newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS-Japan scandal threatens disturbing detour.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Japan scandal threatens disturbing detour.

text.p: Japan's financial scandal saga threatened to take a disturbing detour on Wednesday after a report that executives of Nomura Securities were apparently questioned about stock deals with politicians and bureaucrats.

The report in the financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun said prosecutors appeared to have quizzed the Nomura executives about transactions in shares of a major consumer loan firm prior to its initial public offering in August 1996.
The probe is focusing on whether dubious share transfers had been made to politicians and bureaucrats, the paper said.

A Nomura spokesman said he was unable to comment on whether executives had been questioned, but added that Nomura believed it was handling initial public offering allocations appropriately, based on the rules of the Japan Securities Dealers Association (JSDA).
Nomura is already embroiled in a high-profile scandal -- its second in six years -- over alleged payoffs to a "sokaiya" corporate extortionist.
Payoffs to sokaiya, who typically threaten to disclose corporate misdeeds or disrupt shareholders meetings, have been illegal since 1983, but many firms persisted in the practice.

The sokaiya scandal has led to more than a dozen arrests of officials from Nomura and one of Japan's biggest banks, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, and has besmirched the financial sector's image just as Japan kicks off its "Big Bang" reforms aimed at boosting competition in the industry and its markets.

Allegations that the other three of Japan's Big Four brokerages also had illegal accounts with Ryuichi Koike, the racketeer at the heart of the scandal and helped slice more than two percent off the Nikkei 225 share average on Tuesday.
The same jitters helped push down the market barometer nearly one percent on Wednesday morning and below 20,000 points for the first time in more than a month.
The three brokerages -- Nikko Securities, Daiwa Securities and Yamaichi Securities -- told the JSDA on Tuesday that they had so far not uncovered any illegal deals.

On Wednesday, the mass-circulation daily Sankei Shimbun said that the government's watchdog agency, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission, might file a legal complaint with prosecutors if it found that the brokerages used illegal discretionary accounts to transfer payoffs to the racketeer.

A DKB spokeswoman declined comment on another media report that said the bank had extended loans to other sokaiya groups. The bank said in May when it admitted funding Koike's brother that it might have made improper loans to others.
Japan's biggest consumer finance firm, Takefuji Corp, meanwhile, acknowledged on Wednesday that it was probably the company referred to in the Nihon Keizai Shimbun report.
But a spokesman told Reuters that the company had not been investigated by prosecutors and had done nothing wrong.

Takefuji and the Finance Ministry were embarrassed by news last October that a former Finance Ministry official was offered its shares prior to the public offering. Neither the firm nor the ex-official was accused of breaking any laws and Takefuji said then it saw nothing amiss in the transaction.

Japan's swirling scandal has raised fears of a re-run of a 1991 financial drama of improper deals and fraudulent loans which ensnared nearly all of Japan's top and second-tier brokerages as well as several elite banks.

But pressure on financial firms to clean up corporate ethics is likely to be much greater than after the 1991 scandals, given stepped-up competition from foreign rivals as the "Big Bang" reforms proceed, some analysts said.

"The scandals could mean that the writing is on the wall. Given the new entrants into the financial sector, Japanese firms will either change or get competed out of business," a foreign analyst said. "It's that threat that may cause real changes in behaviour."
